title: Scalars, vectors and interactions
cards: Magnitude and direction

Scalars have magnitude only: distance, speed, mass, time and energy. Vectors also have direction: displacement, velocity, acceleration and force. An arrow shows direction; its length represents magnitude using a stated scale. Turning a velocity arrow changes velocity even when its length stays the same.
Two objects, two forces

A force is a push or pull arising from an interaction. Contact interactions include friction, air resistance, tension and normal contact. Gravity, electrostatic and magnetic interactions act without physical contact. Each object exerts a force on the other; name the objects and what acts on what.
Read a scaled arrow

With 1 cm representing 5 N, a 3 cm arrow represents 15 N in the arrow’s direction. Reversing the arrow reverses the represented force; it does not make its magnitude negative. A signed number can encode direction along a chosen straight-line axis.
Build a vector representation

Choose a 10/20 N force and left/right direction. Predict the signed component when right is positive. The arrow scales with force; the block’s position is not a motion prediction. The model isolates one force and does not assert that a single force is the entire force system.

title: Mass, weight and gravity
cards: Mass is not a force

Mass measures the amount of matter in kilograms; weight is the gravitational force in newtons. A gravitational field gives objects weight even when there is no contact. Moving an object to a different field changes its weight while its mass can remain unchanged.
Use W = mg

Weight W = mass m × field strength g. Use the supplied g in N/kg. For 3 kg with g=9.8 N/kg, W=29.4 N. Weight is directly proportional to mass at fixed g. A calibrated newtonmeter measures weight, not kilograms of mass.
Centre of mass

For force diagrams, the weight can be represented as acting through the centre of mass toward the attracting body. The marker is a simplified whole-object representation, not a statement that all the object’s matter lies at one point.
Compare fields

Choose mass and gravitational field strength. Predict the newtonmeter reading, then reveal. The downward arrow changes in proportion to mg. The demonstration is stationary; support balances weight, and no fall-time calculation is implied.

title: Resultant forces in a straight line
cards: Replace the whole force set

A resultant force has the same effect as the combined forces on the selected object. Choose the object first. Along a straight line, add forces in the same direction and subtract opposing magnitudes. State the direction of a nonzero answer.
Zero resultant does not mean no forces

A rightward 12 N force and leftward 8 N force give 4 N right. Equal opposing forces give zero resultant. A zero resultant means no acceleration: the object may be at rest or already moving at constant velocity.
Avoid mixing objects

A force diagram contains forces on one chosen object. The force that object exerts on another belongs to a different diagram. Two equal opposite interaction forces on different objects do not cancel within one object’s force account.
Balance the arrows

Choose rightward drive and leftward resistance. Predict signed resultant (right positive). Arrows share a scale; no speed is inferred without mass and time. Try both a balanced and unbalanced condition.

title: Force components and scale diagrams
cards: One force, two components

A force may be resolved into two perpendicular components with the same combined effect as the original. Draw the original arrow and a right-angle component rectangle. The original is the diagonal; the component arrows are not extra physical forces.
Construct a resultant

For two forces at an angle, draw them tip-to-tail at a stated scale. The arrow from the first tail to the final tip is the resultant. Measure its length and direction. A closed tip-to-tail polygon indicates equilibrium. AQA requires scale drawings here, not trigonometric recall.

A 3 N horizontal and 4 N vertical pair gives a 5 N diagonal in a familiar scaled example. Its direction is upwards and rightwards. The larger component pulls the resultant direction closer to that axis. A single force can be represented by this equivalent pair.

title: Work done by a force
cards: Force through a displacement

A force does work when it causes displacement along its line of action. Work done W=Fs, with force in N and distance along that force in m. The result is energy transferred in joules. One joule equals one newton-metre of work.
Keep the direction condition

A 20 N force acting through3 m along its direction transfers60 J. A sideways force with no displacement along it does not transfer work through that sideways component. A large static force with zero displacement does no mechanical work on the stationary object.
Friction transfers energy

Work done against friction reduces mechanical energy stores and raises internal energy/temperature of the object and surroundings. Energy is conserved even when the useful mechanical transfer is smaller than the input. Use the existing Energy lessons for the linked store account.
Move a block

Choose constant force and along-force displacement. Predict work. The replay moves a block through a scaled illustrative distance and accumulates transferred energy; it is not a trajectory solved from the forces or a claim of constant acceleration.

title: Elasticity and force–extension graphs
cards: Two forces change shape

A stationary object needs opposing applied forces to stretch, bend or compress it. Elastic deformation reverses when forces are removed. Inelastic deformation leaves a permanent change. The limit of proportionality marks where a force–extension graph stops being a straight line through the origin; it is not a universal synonym for the elastic limit.
Use F = ke in the linear region

Extension e = stretched length − original length, in metres. Spring constant k is force per unit extension, N/m. A spring with k=100 N/m under5 N extends0.05 m. Compression can be treated similarly. A steeper F-versus-e gradient means a larger k.
Energy stored while stretching

If the spring stays within the proportional elastic region, elastic energy E=½ke² equals work done stretching it. The force increases with extension, so multiplying the final force by extension overestimates the work. The energy is the triangular area under the F–e graph.

Choose k and applied force, predict extension, then reveal. The model stays in the stated linear elastic region and returns to its original length on unloading. Coil thickness/diameter are symbolic; the spring is not a material-failure prediction.

title: Investigating force and extension
cards: Plan the spring investigation

Required practical6 in separate Physics and18 in Trilogy investigates force versus extension of a spring. Clamp securely; align a ruler beside the spring with a pointer/reference point. Measure the unloaded length, add known forces in small increments, allow oscillation to settle and read at eye level to reduce parallax.
Control and record

Use the same spring, ruler position and reference point. Record applied force and total length, then calculate extension in metres. Repeat readings where useful. Keep clear of falling masses and avoid overloading; a catch tray helps. Physical school performance is still required.
Interpret the graph

Plot force vertically against extension horizontally with labelled units and a suitable scale. A straight best-fit line through the origin supports F∝e; gradient ΔF/Δe gives k. Do not force all points onto a line beyond proportional behaviour. Unloading can test whether deformation is reversible.

Choose one of two ideal toy springs and extension. Predict force. These generated points have no measurement uncertainty; compare them with real repeated readings and evaluate ruler resolution, zero error, parallax and oscillation. title: Moments, levers and gears
cards: A turning effect

Moment M=F d, where d is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the force’s line of action. Use N m. A longer lever arm can produce the same moment with a smaller force. A force directed through the pivot has zero moment even if applied far along the lever.
Balance clockwise and anticlockwise

A balanced object has equal total clockwise and anticlockwise moments about the pivot. A6 N downward force0.2 m left balances a3 N downward force0.4 m right: both moments are1.2 N m. Include every force with a moment, not just one pair.
Transmit rotation

Levers transmit turning effects. Meshing gears rotate in opposite directions; a smaller gear turns through more revolutions than a larger meshing gear. Changing gear sizes changes turning effect/speed tradeoffs. A simple ideal gear train transfers energy; it does not create energy.
Balance a lever

An opposing moment is fixed at4 N m. Choose force and perpendicular distance on the other side; predict that side’s moment and decide whether it balances. The diagram shows a constrained force direction. Draw your own pivot/line of action/perpendicular distance to demonstrate the unrestricted skill.

title: Fluid pressure and surface forces
cards: Fluids exert normal forces

Liquids and gases are fluids. Pressure produces a force at right angles to a surface. Pressure is force per unit area: p=F/A, in pascals, where1 Pa=1 N/m². A gas can press on side walls and a lid, not only downward.
Separate force and pressure

For the same normal force, a smaller area gives a larger pressure. A200 N normal force across0.5 m² gives400 Pa. To find the total force for a given pressure, rearrange F=pA. Area units must be m²;100 cm²=0.01 m².
Apply the direction condition

Use the component of force normal to the chosen surface. The arrows in this view point outward from fluid toward the container wall; the wall exerts an opposite force on the fluid. Neither force is a sideways friction arrow.
Change force and area

Choose normal force and surface area, predict pressure and reveal. The distribution is uniform in this simplified surface account; the demonstration does not calculate liquid depth, flow, gas compression or material failure.

title: Liquid depth, upthrust and floating
cards: Pressure increases with depth

The pressure due to a liquid column is p=hρg. Use column height/depth h in m, densityρ in kg/m³ and supplied g in N/kg. This is the additional liquid pressure; add surface pressure if asked for absolute pressure. Denser liquid or greater depth gives larger pressure.
A pressure difference gives upthrust

A submerged object has greater pressure on its bottom than its top. The vertical force difference gives upward upthrust; opposing horizontal forces can cancel. Upthrust depends on displaced fluid. The diagram exaggerates vertical pressure differences for clarity.
Float or sink

An unsupported object initially sinks if weight exceeds upthrust and rises if upthrust exceeds weight. It floats at rest when upthrust balances weight. A floating object displaces its own weight of fluid. Average object density and fluid density help decide whether it can float; shape affects the displaced volume.
Compare liquid columns

Choose depth and density with supplied g=10 N/kg. Predict pressure due to the column. The static model has no waves, viscosity or compressibility; it does not predict transient sinking speed. Use different depths to explain the pressure difference around a block.

title: Atmospheric pressure and altitude
cards: A thin layer around Earth

The atmosphere is a thin layer compared with Earth’s size. Air molecules continually move and collide with surfaces, producing atmospheric pressure. The atmosphere is denser closer to the ground and becomes less dense at higher altitudes.
Less air above

At a higher altitude there are fewer air molecules and less weight of air above each unit area. Atmospheric pressure therefore decreases with altitude. Pressure does not suddenly become zero at the top of a building; the change depends on the height and atmospheric conditions.
Use evidence carefully

Compare measured pressure at different heights while considering weather changes and instrument calibration. The gas particles are greatly enlarged and only a few are drawn. Their collisions represent a mechanism, not a literal number of air molecules.
Read a supplied altitude comparison

title: Distance, displacement, speed and velocity
cards: A journey has two measures

Distance is total path length, a scalar. Displacement is the straight-line change from start to finish with direction, a vector. Walk3 m east then3 m west: distance6 m, displacement0. Speed is scalar; velocity is speed in a stated direction.
Use distance = speed × time

For constant speed, s=vt. Average speed for a variable journey is total distance divided by total time, including stated stops. Do not simply average two speeds unless the time intervals are equal. Convert km/h to m/s by dividing by3.6.
Estimate sensible speeds

Typical walking speed is1.5 m/s, running3 m/s, cycling6 m/s and sound in air about330 m/s. Terrain, fitness, age and journey length affect human speeds. A car on a road may travel around13 m/s (about30 mph), while other transport varies widely. These are estimates, not universal constants.
Compare simple journeys

Choose constant speed and elapsed time. Predict total distance before watching a straight-line journey. The markers show equally spaced positions for equal times. A later return leg can change displacement without undoing the distance already travelled.

extra.title: Higher: constant speed can still change velocity
extra.text: An object moving in a circle changes direction continuously even at constant speed. Its velocity changes, so it accelerates. The resultant force is toward the centre; it is perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity, not a force pushing the object outward.

title: Reading distance–time graphs
cards: A slope tells you speed

On a distance–time graph, gradient = change in distance ÷ change in time. A steeper positive line means greater speed. A horizontal section means no further distance travelled during that time. A straight sloping line represents constant speed.
Construct from measurements

Choose sensible axis ranges, plot time horizontally and distance vertically with units, and plot measured points. A line or smooth curve should fit the evidence. Use a large gradient triangle, reading two points on the line rather than assuming it starts at the origin.
Curves represent changing speed

A curve getting steeper represents increasing speed; a curve getting flatter represents decreasing speed. Total distance cannot decrease in a cumulative-distance account. A position/displacement graph can decrease, but that is a different vertical quantity.
Compare slopes

Choose a distance increment and time interval; predict gradient in m/s and reveal the graph. This is constrained graph interpretation. It prepares for drawing and analysing your own measured graph, but does not itself provide unrestricted graph-construction evidence.

title: Acceleration and uniform-motion calculations
cards: Velocity changes per second

Average acceleration a=(v−u)/t. Units are m/s². Choose a positive direction first. A vehicle changing from2 to14 m/s in4 s has acceleration3 m/s². Slowing while moving in the positive direction gives negative acceleration; the magnitude of deceleration is positive.
A second relationship

For uniform acceleration, v²−u²=2as. Rearrange carefully and use SI units. With u=0, a=2 m/s² and s=9 m, v²=36 and speed=6 m/s. The relationship assumes constant acceleration; it cannot be applied indiscriminately to a whole nonuniform journey.
Free fall and resistance

Near Earth, free-fall acceleration is about9.8 m/s² when gravity is the only significant force. Falling through air is not always free fall: air resistance changes the resultant. Everyday accelerations vary; reaching20 m/s from rest in10 s is about2 m/s² on average.
Predict a velocity change

The model starts from rest with constant acceleration. Choose a and time; predict final velocity. Position follows½at² while velocity follows at. Model time resets on replay; the object is not physically teleported back during one continuous journey.

title: Velocity–time graphs
cards: Gradient gives acceleration

On a velocity–time graph, gradient=(change in velocity)/(change in time). A horizontal line means constant velocity, not stationary unless velocity is zero. A downward slope can show slowing in the positive direction. Read signs as well as steepness.
Plot the measured motion

Place time on the horizontal axis and velocity on the vertical axis, with scales and units. Plot supplied measurements, then interpret segments or a best-fit curve. At a curved section, a tangent estimates instantaneous acceleration. A straight slope represents uniform acceleration.
Distinguish the two graph types

Distance–time gradient gives speed; velocity–time gradient gives acceleration. Their vertical quantities differ. Do not read the height of a velocity–time graph as distance. A velocity can be negative because direction is encoded by the chosen axis.

title: Falling objects and terminal velocity
cards: Forces change during a fall

A falling object initially has weight greater than air resistance, so it accelerates downward. As speed increases, air resistance rises and the downward resultant decreases. Weight remains approximately constant for the same mass and gravitational field.
Reach a balanced speed

At terminal velocity, drag balances weight and resultant force is zero. Acceleration is zero, but the object is still moving. A larger drag at a given speed, such as an opened parachute, can give a lower terminal speed. Immediately after opening, upward drag can exceed weight and the falling object slows.
Read the motion

A velocity–time trace initially gets less steep as acceleration decreases and approaches a horizontal terminal-speed region. The supplied curve is an original qualitative shape, not measured parachute data. In separate Physics you should draw and interpret such a graph and connect it to the force account.

Choose weight and drag, predict signed downward resultant and reveal. These selected states do not solve a complete fluid model. A nonzero upward resultant can occur while velocity is still downward: force changes velocity, not necessarily its instantaneous direction.

title: Newton’s first law and inertia
cards: Keep a constant velocity

If the resultant force is zero, a stationary object stays at rest and a moving object continues at the same speed in the same direction. A force is needed to change velocity, not to keep an ideal object moving at constant velocity.
Balance a real vehicle

A car at steady speed has drive balancing resistance. Turning a corner changes direction and therefore velocity, so it requires a resultant even if speed stays the same. Friction explains why everyday coasting objects slow when drive is removed.
Explain the interaction

Identify the chosen object and all important forces on it. Ask whether the vector sum is zero. A book resting on a table has balanced support and weight on the book; these are not Newton’s third-law partners because both act on the same object.
Remove the drive

Choose an ideal resistance-free track or a resistive track, then drive balanced with resistance or drive removed. Predict whether velocity stays constant or changes. The film shows an ideal no-resultant coast; it deliberately omits friction.

extra.title: Higher: inertia
extra.text: Inertia is the tendency of an object to remain at rest or continue in uniform straight-line motion. It does not mean a new force pushes the object forward. When a bus brakes, an unrestrained passenger tends to keep moving; a restraint exerts a force to change that motion.

title: Newton’s second law
cards: Resultant force causes acceleration
F=ma links resultant force in N, mass in kg and acceleration in m/s². The acceleration is in the resultant force’s direction. Use the resultant, not just the driving force when resistance is present.
Change one variable at a time

At fixed mass, acceleration is proportional to resultant force. At fixed resultant force it is inversely proportional to mass: doubling mass halves acceleration. A6 N resultant on2 kg gives3 m/s². The proportionality symbol is ∝.
Estimate real motions

A1000 kg car accelerating at2 m/s² requires about2000 N resultant. Actual drive must also overcome resistance. Estimates depend on supplied mass, interval and assumptions; they are not exact engine ratings.
Predict the acceleration

Choose resultant force and trolley mass, predict a=F/m, then watch a from-rest trajectory with that acceleration. Total mass is the moving system’s mass. The illustrative track has no unmodelled resistance.

extra.text: Inertial mass measures how difficult it is to change velocity. It is defined as the ratio of resultant force to acceleration, m=F/a, for a consistent system and direction. A12 N resultant producing3 m/s² implies inertial mass4 kg. It is not a separate force resisting motion.

Keep total mass controlled

When moving masses from trolley to hanger, the total moving mass can remain constant while the driving force changes. For the mass comparison, change total moving mass but maintain the same driving force. Keep track slope/alignment and release method controlled and reduce friction.
Collect and evaluate

title: Newton’s third law
cards: Interactions come in pairs

When two objects interact, each exerts an equal-magnitude opposite-direction force on the other. Both forces are the same interaction type and act at the same time, on different objects. A larger object does not exert the larger member of the pair.
Name what acts on what

A hand pushes a wall; the wall pushes the hand oppositely. Earth pulls a falling object; the object pulls Earth oppositely. Equal forces can give very different accelerations because the masses differ. Do not put both forces in one object’s free-body diagram.
Equilibrium is a different account

Weight and support can balance on a stationary book, but their partners are book-on-Earth and book-on-table. Balanced forces act on the same object and may be different types; third-law partners act on different objects and are the same type.

title: Thinking distance, reaction time and stopping
cards: Two parts of stopping

Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance. During reaction time the vehicle is still travelling before braking begins. At roughly constant speed, thinking distance = speed × reaction time. Braking distance begins when the brakes act.
Reaction time varies

Typical human reaction times are about0.2–0.9 s. Tiredness, drugs/alcohol and distractions can increase reaction time. Measure with a ruler-drop test or a computer/light response test; control anticipation and practise effects, repeat and compare variability. A ruler measures fall distance, which must be converted to time using a supplied relationship.
Road and vehicle conditions

Wet/icy roads and poor tyres/brakes can increase braking distance by reducing effective braking. They need not increase the driver’s intrinsic reaction time. Higher speed increases thinking distance and usually braking distance. Compare supplied emergency-stop graphs for different vehicles/conditions; values are not interchangeable universal rules.
Watch the thinking interval

title: Braking, energy and deceleration
cards: Transfer kinetic energy

Brake friction transfers energy from the vehicle’s kinetic store to internal energy of brakes and surroundings; brake temperature rises. Work done by an approximately constant braking force is Fs. Setting that equal to½mv² gives an ideal stopping-energy account.
Speed matters strongly

For fixed mass and braking force, doubling speed gives four times the initial kinetic energy and four times the ideal braking distance. Real road grip, brake/tyre condition and weather alter the available force. These assumptions must be stated when interpreting a squared-speed trend.
Deceleration and control

For a given distance, greater speed requires greater braking force. Larger braking force gives larger deceleration. Very large deceleration can cause loss of control and brakes can overheat. A generated energy comparison cannot establish safe stopping distances for a real journey.

title: Momentum and conservation
cards: Mass times velocity
Momentum p=mv, in kg m/s. It is a vector, so choose positive direction and include signs. A2 kg trolley at3 m/s has momentum6 kg m/s. Equal speeds do not imply equal momentum if masses differ.
Define the closed system

Total momentum before an event equals total momentum after if the system has no resultant external force during it. The interaction forces between objects are internal; they redistribute momentum without changing the system total. Momentum conservation does not require kinetic energy conservation in every collision.
Explain a collision

If a moving trolley hits a stationary one, momentum can transfer to it. In a sticking collision the combined mass moves more slowly than the original trolley for equal masses. In explosions, opposite signed momenta can sum to the initial total. Direction signs prevent adding magnitudes incorrectly.

title: Calculating collision and recoil momentum
cards: Write before equals after

For an isolated two-object event, m₁u₁+m₂u₂=m₁v₁+m₂v₂ along a chosen positive direction. Include both objects and signs. This numerical collision-solving requirement is separate Physics Higher; Trilogy uses the conservation concept.
A sticking example

A2 kg trolley at3 m/s sticks to a stationary4 kg trolley. Initial momentum6 kg m/s equals6v afterwards, so v=1 m/s. Check that units are kg m/s and final velocity is plausible. Kinetic energy decreases; momentum still balances.
Recoil and opposite directions

An initially stationary system has total momentum zero. If a1 kg object leaves at+4 m/s, the remaining2 kg must have−4 kg m/s and velocity−2 m/s. Opposite signs matter; do not conserve scalar speeds. Real external forces may make a chosen system only approximately isolated.

title: Force, momentum change and protection
cards: Change momentum over time

A resultant force changes momentum. Average force F=Δp/Δt, in newtons. Use final momentum minus initial momentum and a consistent positive direction. A2 kg object slowing from10 m/s to rest changes momentum by−20 kg m/s.
Spread the change over longer time

For the same momentum change, increasing collision time reduces average force. Seat belts, airbags, crumple zones and landing mats increase stopping time/distance while restraining or cushioning motion. They do not remove the momentum change required to stop an object.
Evaluate a protection claim

A force calculated from Δp/Δt is an average, not necessarily the peak. Compare supplied time, force and injury-related evidence; a longer stopping interval alone does not guarantee every outcome. Protection must restrain the object effectively and avoid additional hazards.
